sections.heading: Aristotle's The Athenian Constitution
paragraphs: This is the Greek text of Ἀθηναίων πολιτεία (conventionally "The Athenian Constitution").

This work's authenticity is disputed by modern scholarship: it has long been transmitted under Aristotle's name, but whether he is its actual author (as opposed to a work by a close associate or early member of his school, later attributed to him) remains an open question - stated here plainly, as scholarship states it, not silently assumed either way.

The text here is Greek only, verbatim. Nothing is translated, modernised, normalised or silently corrected beyond the documented resolution of the source's own apparatus markup (see "How it was imported" below). Where the source is irregular or a genuine judgement call was made, it is preserved/recorded and flagged in "Known gaps & anomalies" below.

sections.heading: English translation
paragraphs: An English translation of this work is in scope for a separate, concurrently-run import task covering select works of this reader; see this data directory's sibling `-en` work (if present) for its own about.json and provenance. This Greek import does not itself depend on that translation existing.

sections.heading: The edition
paragraphs: Per this XML file's own <sourceDesc>: Aristotelis Atheniensium Respublica (Kenyon, ed., Clarendon Press, 1920), Oxford, 1920.

Discovered only in 1890 (on an Egyptian papyrus), so it carries no Bekker page citation at all - Kenyon's own chapter numbering (1-69, plus a handful of numbered fragments of the lost opening, e.g. "frag_2") is the only citation scheme and is used here as-is for Division.number.

sections.heading: Digital source
paragraphs: The machine-readable text is the TEI XML file tlg0086.tlg003.perseus-grc2.xml (CTS urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0086.tlg003.perseus-grc2) from the Perseus Digital Library / Open Greek and Latin canonical-greekLit repository. It was fetched once and is bundled with the app (scripts/import-aristotle-rest/raw/tlg0086.tlg003.perseus-grc2.xml); nothing is loaded from the network at runtime.

sections.heading: How it was imported
paragraphs: The importer's generic TEI walker (scripts/import-aristotle-rest-shared/teiWalker.ts) parses this source's own <div type="textpart" subtype="..." n="..."> nesting into a tree, and shapes.ts folds it onto this app's Division scheme: a flat list of Chapters (id `ch-N`, rendered "§ N") - the source has no Book-level division; deeper source nesting below the "section" level, if any, is folded into each Chapter's own Passage array rather than adding another Division level.

... (text an editor judged spurious/interpolated, but which the edition still PRINTS, bracketed - the OCT convention) is KEPT verbatim in the reading text, wrapped in square brackets `[...]` (or left unbracketed-but-verbatim on the rare occasion its own printed text already contains a literal bracket, so as not to double them); / keeps the reading and excludes the variant; a bare (no offered) is itself the edition's printed reading and is kept, logged as a crux; ... (an editorial insertion, printed by the edition) is KEPT inline; ... (a modern editorial citation, not Aristotle's own words) is EXCLUDED; / a Bekker-shaped is captured to build Division.ref and removed from the reading prose; any OTHER is discarded entirely (tag and content); a is kept as its literal printed ellipsis text, a contributes no text; ////////<item>/<list>/<cit> (quotations, verse, foreign-language snippets, emphasis, numerals, a quoted work's title, list/table items) are unwrapped - tags stripped, text kept inline as ordinary reading prose, WHETHER nested inside a <p> or printed as a sibling of one (a verse quotation is very often the latter - e.g. this corpus's Empedocles/Homer citations - and is captured as its own implicit paragraph rather than dropped). Every occurrence of all of these except plain milestones/lb/pb is logged in anomalies.json. Entities are decoded and text is NFC-normalised and whitespace-collapsed; the words themselves are otherwise untouched.

In this file: 0 <del> span(s) bracket-kept, 56 <add> insertion(s) kept, 0 bare <sic> crux(es) kept, 0 <choice><sic> variant(s) excluded in favour of <corr>, 1 literal-ellipsis <gap>(s) kept, 25 lacuna <gap>(s) excluded, 11 non-citation <note>(s) discarded.

sections.heading: Reference scheme
paragraphs: This source carries no inline Bekker page/column citation of its own (verified: neither <note type="marginal"> nor a Bekker-shaped <milestone> occurs anywhere in the body) - Division.ref is null throughout, logged once as a work-level anomaly rather than per-chapter. Citation here is by Chapter number alone.

No printed sub-chapter/line-level reference is attempted for any individual Passage (Passage.ref is null throughout); where a source nests a nameable level below its Chapter (e.g. a "section"), that level's own number survives as Passage.n (e.g. "3", or "3.2" two levels down) rather than being discarded.

sections.heading: Known gaps & anomalies
paragraphs: All 73 Chapter(s) and 309 Passage(s) (106338 characters of Greek reading text) present in this source were imported; nothing was dropped except the documented apparatus exclusions above, and no paragraph was reordered or merged beyond the documented Book/Chapter folding.

Discovered only in 1890 (on an Egyptian papyrus), so it carries no Bekker page citation at all - Kenyon's own chapter numbering (1-69, plus a handful of numbered fragments of the lost opening, e.g. "frag_2") is the only citation scheme and is used here as-is for Division.number.
